notes: Tuesday 24 Nov 2026 world issue (Taipei ~08:00). Window: Sun 22 – Mon 23 Nov (US/Europe). Economy: Nvidia reinstates Jensen Huang, stock +31%; Fed's Williams hints at more hikes over time; Asia props up markets; Europe gas jumps on cold snap. Tech: US to blacklist Megaspeed; CrowdStrike buys Zscaler for $44bn; Oregon and Virginia sue SpaceX over Grok deepfakes; 150+ groups urge Amazon/eBay to stop selling AI toys. Politics: Belgium austerity strike; India pledges $1.6bn to Nepal; Kenya and DR Congo restore ties; Burnham says no EU return without referendum. Literature (US): PEN Writes US splinter group; Richard Russo on his panic attack; The Sun Also Rises at 100; Anya Jabour on the first study of women's sex lives. Society: Oxfam calls Gaza a toxic wasteland; Iranian singer flogged over hijab; smart cars used in domestic abuse; Nigeria boat disaster.

stories.headline: Nvidia brings Jensen Huang back as CEO; its stock jumps 31% in one day
stories.dek: Eleven days after he quit over an affair scandal, the board voted him back. Trump says he "made the deal."
stories.caveman: Nvidia makes the chips that power most of the world's AI, and it is one of the most valuable companies on Earth. Its founder, Jensen Huang, quit as CEO on Nov. 12 after reports of affairs, including one with Alice Huang (no relation), a former executive at a Singapore company whom US intelligence suspects of working for China. China denies she is a spy. On Monday, Nvidia's board voted unanimously to bring him back. The board said it had talked with Huang, was satisfied with his honesty, and had heard from senior US government officials that his return poses no national security risk. President Trump told CNBC he spoke to the board and convinced them, and that Huang "did nothing wrong." Investors cheered: Nvidia's stock closed up 31% on Monday, after losing about a third of its value since Huang admitted the affair on Nov. 8. Other tech stocks rallied too. The board's own investigation into Huang is still going on.
stories.why_it_matters: Nvidia is so big that its stock moves the whole market, including many people's retirement funds. Last week's crash was partly about Nvidia losing its leader. One man's return just added hundreds of billions of dollars in value in one day.
stories.camps: Supporters, including many investors, employees and tech leaders like Elon Musk, say Huang is irreplaceable and the board fixed a mistake. Critics, including Democratic senators like Elizabeth Warren and some Republicans, say it was reckless to bring him back before the national security questions are answered, and they question why the president got involved in a private company's hiring. Huang is due to testify publicly to a Senate committee on Dec. 3.
stories.image_alt: Jensen Huang on stage at Nvidia's GTC conference in San Jose, California, in March 2026

terms.explain: Chief executive officer: the top boss who runs a company day to day.
A group of people chosen to represent shareholders. They can hire and fire the CEO.
A small piece of ownership in a company. Its price goes up when more people want to buy it.
A danger to a country's safety, for example secrets or technology reaching a rival government.

stories.headline: Top Fed official: more interest rate rises are likely "over time" to beat inflation
stories.dek: New York Fed chief John Williams says getting prices under control is "100% essential," but he prefers a slow, steady approach.
stories.caveman: The Federal Reserve (the Fed) is America's central bank. One of its main tools is the interest rate: raising it makes borrowing more expensive, which cools spending and slows price rises (inflation). On Monday, John Williams, head of the New York Fed and one of its most influential voices, said the Fed still has "work to do" to bring inflation back to its 2% goal. He said the Fed must "take actions over time" to get there, which markets read as a hint of more rate rises, but at a measured pace. He blamed today's price pressure on the war involving Iran, heavy demand for goods linked to the AI building boom, and tariffs, though he said the tariff effect has mostly faded. He expects inflation to get close to 2% in 2027 and reach it in 2028. He also said there is "little evidence" AI will cause long-lasting inflation. On Monday, the yield on 2-year US government bonds jumped as investors waited for his speech.
stories.why_it_matters: Fed rates affect mortgage costs, credit cards, car loans and savings around the world. Higher US rates also pull money out of markets like Taiwan's and can weaken currencies like the NT dollar.
stories.camps: Some Fed officials want faster, bigger rate rises to crush inflation quickly. Others, like Williams, worry that going too fast could hurt jobs and the economy, so they prefer small steps. Many households care most about prices, while businesses and borrowers worry about higher loan costs.
stories.image_alt: New York Fed President John Williams speaking at an Economic Club of New York event in 2025

terms.explain: The central bank of the United States. It sets key interest rates and watches over banks.
When prices for everyday things keep rising, so the same money buys less.
The price of borrowing money, shown as a percent per year.
The interest the US government pays on its bonds. It rises when investors expect higher Fed rates.

stories.headline: Asia's governments step in to stop a tech-stock crash: Korea readies a rescue fund, Taiwan bans short-selling
stories.dek: South Korea, Taiwan and China each took new steps as the AI sell-off spilled into another week.
stories.caveman: Stocks in Asia's tech-heavy markets have been hit hard by fears that the AI boom is a bubble. Governments are now trying different fixes. South Korea, where the Kospi index has fallen more than 46% from its June high, said it is getting a market stabilization fund of about $8 billion ready to buy stocks, will let companies buy back more of their own shares, and will watch closely for illegal short-selling. Taiwan's financial regulator banned most short-selling below the previous day's closing price, raised the cost of short bets, and urged companies to buy back their own stock. Taiwan's market had dropped 17.5% last week, with TSMC down 15%. China went the other way: instead of limiting bets, its stock exchanges will let investors borrow more to buy shares, starting Nov. 30, and cut trading fees. On Monday, Korea's Kospi fell another 3.26%, while Taiwan's index turned around and rose over 2%.
stories.why_it_matters: These moves affect anyone with savings in Asian stocks or funds. They also show how much this region's economies now depend on a few AI chip companies.
stories.camps: Supporters say emergency steps calm panic and stop a crash from feeding on itself. Critics argue that short-selling bans and government buying can hide real problems, make markets less honest, and delay a needed correction. China's plan to let people borrow more is especially risky, they say, because borrowed money makes losses bigger.
stories.image_alt: Currency dealers at Hana Bank in Seoul in front of a screen showing South Korea's Kospi stock index

terms.explain: Borrowing shares and selling them, hoping to buy them back cheaper later. It is a bet that prices will fall.
Money set aside to buy stocks during a crash to slow the fall.
When a company buys its own shares, which can support the price.
When prices fall 20% or more from a recent high.

stories.headline: Europe's gas prices jump as a cold snap nears and storage runs low
stories.dek: Gas storage is only about 69% full, versus a normal 80%. UK bills could rise 26% from January.
stories.caveman: Many homes in Europe use natural gas for heating, and winter is when they need it most. On Monday, the main European gas price jumped as much as 8.6% before ending up 4%, because weather forecasters expect a cold spell in north-west Europe in the coming weeks. Supplies are already tight. Exports from Qatar, a big gas seller, have slowed because of the war in the Middle East, and Europe burned extra gas over a long, hot summer to run cooling. Storage tanks across the continent are about 69% full, compared with a typical 80% at this time of year. In the UK, officials say there will be enough energy, but only because Britain pays higher prices than its neighbors to win imports. The energy regulator Ofgem is expected to raise its price cap 26% from January, about £443 more a year for an average home. The charity Citizens Advice warns that millions of households are "entering the coldest months of the year with nothing left."
stories.why_it_matters: Energy bills hit poorer families hardest, because heating and food take up a bigger part of their budget. High gas prices also push up prices of many other goods.
stories.camps: Charities and opposition voices want more targeted help, like bigger discounts for vulnerable homes and emergency credit for prepaid meters. The UK government points to its £100 energy bill top-up for 20 million homes. Some economists say Europe must cut its dependence on imported gas faster; others say that switch costs money people don't have right now.
stories.image_alt: A person walks a dog across a snowy field in north-west Europe
stories.image_credit: Photo: Owen Humphreys/PA via The Guardian

terms.explain: A fossil fuel used for heating homes, cooking and making electricity.
A government limit on how much energy companies can charge households per unit.
A short period of unusually cold weather.
Big underground tanks where countries keep gas for winter.

stories.headline: US moves to blacklist Megaspeed, the company tied to the Nvidia spy scandal
stories.dek: The Commerce Department says it has investigated the Singapore-based data center firm for nearly two years over Nvidia chips reaching China.
stories.caveman: The US Commerce Department said it plans to add Megaspeed, a data center company based in Singapore, to its "entity list," a blacklist that blocks trade with US firms. Its subsidiary Speedmatrix is also on the list. The department said it has been investigating Megaspeed for almost two years, suspecting it helped get Nvidia's powerful AI chips into China, which the US has blocked from buying such chips since 2022. Megaspeed bought billions of dollars of Nvidia chips, and the Chinese tech giant Alibaba has reportedly been one of its biggest customers. Megaspeed became famous only last month, when reports said a former executive, Alice Huang, had an affair with Nvidia boss Jensen Huang, and US intelligence believes she worked for Beijing. China denies she is a spy and warned the US not to use the scandal as an excuse for a "technological blockade." The date the ban starts was not given.
stories.why_it_matters: AI chips are now treated like strategic weapons. Where they end up affects the US-China rivalry, and Taiwan sits in the middle, since TSMC makes most of these chips.
stories.camps: Supporters of tough export controls say this proves chips are slipping into China through other countries and the rules need teeth. Critics, including many in the chip industry, argue that bans hurt US companies' sales and push China to build its own chips faster. China calls the controls an unfair attempt to hold back its development.
stories.image_alt: The Megaspeed logo on a wall at the company's offices

terms.explain: A US government blacklist. American companies need special permission to sell to anyone on it.
Government rules that limit selling certain goods, like advanced chips, to certain countries.
A huge building full of computers that run websites and AI.
A company that is owned by another company.

stories.headline: CrowdStrike to buy Zscaler for $44 billion as AI makes hacking easier
stories.dek: It's CrowdStrike's biggest deal ever, combining two big cybersecurity companies after a wave of major outages and hacks.
stories.caveman: CrowdStrike, a big American cybersecurity company based in Austin, Texas, plans to buy rival Zscaler for $43.9 billion. It will pay in its own shares, not cash: Zscaler owners will get 1.135 CrowdStrike shares for each Zscaler share. CrowdStrike protects computers and devices; Zscaler protects network connections. Together they want to be the biggest "AI safety and security company the world has ever seen," CrowdStrike CEO George Kurtz said. The deal comes as AI tools help attackers find and exploit software weaknesses faster, and after recent outages at Microsoft, the US aviation agency FAA and JPMorgan Chase. On Monday, Zscaler's stock rose nearly 18% and CrowdStrike's fell 9%. Together the two were worth more than $265 billion, just behind leader Palo Alto Networks. The deal is expected to close in the second half of CrowdStrike's 2028 fiscal year.
stories.why_it_matters: Banks, hospitals, airlines and governments all rely on these companies. When security tools fail, or a hack succeeds, everyday services can stop working.
stories.camps: Supporters say one bigger platform is simpler and stronger for customers facing AI-powered attacks. Skeptics warn that fewer, bigger security companies mean less competition and higher prices, and a single failure could affect many more customers at once. CrowdStrike's own stock drop shows some investors think it is paying too much.
stories.image_alt: Photo illustration of the Zscaler logo on a phone in front of the CrowdStrike logo
stories.image_credit: Photo illustration: Getty Images via CNBC

terms.explain: Protecting computers, networks and data from hackers.
When one company buys another.
Paying for a company with your own shares instead of cash.
When a service or system stops working.

stories.headline: Oregon and Virginia become first states to sue SpaceX over Grok AI deepfake porn
stories.dek: The states say Grok and X let users make and spread fake sexual images of real people, including children, without enough safeguards.
stories.caveman: SpaceX, Elon Musk's company, now owns the AI chatbot Grok and the social network X. On Monday, Oregon and Virginia became the first US states to sue it over Grok's image tools. Research by groups like the Internet Watch Foundation found that Grok and X have let users create and share explicit "deepfakes" made from real photos of people, including children, who never agreed. The state attorneys general say SpaceX failed to put proper safeguards in place and falsely presented its apps as generally safe, which they say breaks consumer protection laws. They note that X lets users as young as 13 on the platform. SpaceX said that when people try to break its safeguards, it takes action, including closing accounts and telling police, and that trying to make such material is a serious crime. SpaceX already faces other lawsuits and investigations over Grok in the UK, Spain, Ireland, France and California.
stories.why_it_matters: AI can now make a fake nude image of anyone from one normal photo. Most victims are women and girls. Who is responsible, the user or the company that built the tool, is one of the biggest legal questions of the AI era.
stories.camps: The states and child safety groups say companies must build safety in from the start and be held responsible for harm. SpaceX says it already has strict controls and that the people who misuse the tools are the criminals. In an earlier lawsuit by the city of Baltimore, the company pointed to Section 230, a US law that often protects platforms from being sued over what users post, so these cases may face a tough legal fight.
stories.image_alt: Photo illustration of the Grok logo in front of the word "deepfake"
stories.image_credit: Photo illustration: Getty Images via CNBC

terms.explain: A fake photo, video or audio made with AI that looks real.
The top legal officer of a US state; can sue companies on behalf of the public.
Rules that stop companies from lying to or harming customers.
A US law that often shields websites from lawsuits over content their users post.

stories.headline: 150+ child safety groups tell Amazon and eBay: stop selling AI toys this Christmas
stories.dek: Testers found AI-powered toys saying unsafe things to kids; one plush bunny linked to ChatGPT was sold for ages 3 and up.
stories.caveman: AI toys are stuffed animals and robots with a chatbot inside, so they can talk with children. More than 150 child safety groups and experts on six continents, including US and UK groups and Jonathan Haidt's Anxious Generation movement, sent a letter to the bosses of Amazon and eBay asking them to stop selling AI toys until they are proven safe, and to refund buyers. In one test by a UK group, a plush bunny listed for ages 3 and up, but connected to ChatGPT (whose own rules require users to be 13+), told a child they could agree to being touched for pleasure. Amazon removed it, but it came back under a different seller before being removed again. About 50 AI toys were recently found for sale on Amazon in the US. Last week, the US Public Interest Research Group tested seven AI toys and found most were too faulty to sell, with privacy problems and inappropriate answers; one secretly took photos.
stories.why_it_matters: These toys talk to very young children who trust them completely. They can also record voices and collect data inside the home.
stories.camps: Safety groups say the "precautionary principle" should apply: prove a product is safe before it reaches kids, not pull it after harm is found. Toy makers and some tech fans say AI toys can help with learning and company, and that rules should target bad products, not ban the whole category. Amazon removed specific listings but has not announced a wider ban.
stories.image_alt: AI-powered toys tested by the US Public Interest Research Group, including plush animals and a small robot
stories.image_credit: Photo: Rory Erlich/AP via The Guardian

terms.explain: A toy with a built-in chatbot that can hold conversations.
A computer program that talks with people in normal language.
The idea that something should be proven safe before it is widely used.
Public Interest Research Group, a US consumer watchdog that tests products.

stories.headline: Belgium grinds to a halt: strike against budget cuts grounds 400+ flights
stories.dek: Unions oppose plans to cut pensions and health spending as Prime Minister Bart De Wever struggles to hold his coalition together.
stories.caveman: Belgium's unions held a national strike on Monday against the government's planned austerity (spending cuts). Air traffic controllers walked out, so no flights took off or landed at Brussels Airport for most of the day: 404 flights were canceled, affecting more than 50,000 passengers. Charleroi airport also stopped. The Brussels metro shut down, and schools and other public services were disrupted as tens of thousands marched in the capital. Prime Minister Bart De Wever is trying to pass a budget that cuts borrowing. His five-party coalition is stuck because one party, the socialist Vooruit, wants higher taxes on the rich and smaller cuts to pensions and health care. De Wever offered to resign earlier this month, but King Philippe refused and told him to keep negotiating. Union leaders called for a "genuine wealth tax" instead of "dismantling the social protection system."
stories.why_it_matters: Many countries face the same hard choice: how to cut debt without hurting ordinary people. Belgium shows how strikes and fragile coalitions shape that fight.
stories.camps: The government and its supporters say Belgium's debt is too high and cuts are needed to keep borrowing costs from rising. Unions and the left say workers and patients should not pay the price, and the rich should pay more tax. Stranded travelers and businesses complain about the disruption.
stories.image_alt: A few travelers at Brussels Airport in front of a departures board, with no flights leaving

terms.explain: Government cuts to spending, often to reduce debt.
When several parties share power because none won enough seats alone.
When workers across many industries stop working at the same time in protest.
A tax on the total assets of very rich people, not just their income.

stories.headline: India pledges $1.6bn to flood-hit Nepal as its young PM seeks a reset
stories.dek: Nepal's 36-year-old Prime Minister Balen Shah, who rose to power after Gen Z-led protests, met Narendra Modi in Delhi.
stories.caveman: Nepal is a small mountain country between two giants, India and China. Its Prime Minister, Balen Shah, is 36 and came to power after protests led by young people (Gen Z) toppled the previous leader. He has said Nepal wants to be treated as an equal by its powerful neighbors. On his first visit to India's capital, he met Prime Minister Narendra Modi, 76. The two exchanged gifts and launched a new cross-border train service. They signed deals on trade, hydropower, transport and education for young Nepalis. Most importantly, India announced a $1.6 billion support package to help Nepal recover from floods in September that killed more than 1,400 people, with thousands still missing. Nepal estimates rebuilding could cost up to $4.8 billion. Shah's government has been criticized at home for its support to families who lost homes and loved ones.
stories.why_it_matters: Small countries next to big powers often have to balance between them. India's aid is also about competing with China for influence in Nepal.
stories.camps: Supporters in Nepal say the money is badly needed and better ties with India help trade and jobs. Critics worry about depending too much on India and want Nepal to keep good ties with China too. In India, some see the aid as smart diplomacy; others question its cost.
stories.image_alt: Nepal's Prime Minister Balen Shah and India's Prime Minister Narendra Modi shake hands in Delhi

terms.explain: People born roughly from the late 1990s to the early 2010s.
Electricity made from flowing water, often from dams.
Money and help one country gives another.

stories.headline: Kenya and DR Congo agree to restore full ties after a fight over rebel groups
stories.dek: Relations broke down in 2023 when Congo accused Kenya of hosting the launch of a rebel alliance that includes M23.
stories.caveman: The Democratic Republic of Congo (DR Congo) has been fighting rebel groups in its east for years; the strongest is M23. In 2023, a political-military alliance that includes M23 was launched in Kenya's capital, Nairobi. DR Congo was angry, accused Kenya of hosting rebel leaders, and pulled its ambassador out of Kenya. On Sunday, Kenya's President William Ruto and DR Congo's President Félix Tshisekedi met in Oyo, a town in the neighboring Republic of Congo, and agreed to restore full diplomatic ties. They promised to respect each other's borders, not interfere in each other's affairs, and settle disputes peacefully. The meeting was hosted by Congo-Brazzaville's President Denis Sassou Nguesso, with Togo's leader as mediator. DR Congo also accuses Rwanda of backing M23; Rwanda denies this despite what the BBC calls overwhelming evidence.
stories.why_it_matters: The war in eastern Congo has forced millions of people from their homes. Peace between neighbors is one small step toward ending it.
stories.camps: Supporters say talking is better than freezing each other out, and East African unity matters for trade. Skeptics note that many past deals in the region failed, and the fighting on the ground has not stopped. Some in Congo remain suspicious of Kenya's role.
stories.image_alt: Kenya's President William Ruto, DR Congo's President Félix Tshisekedi and Congo-Brazzaville's President Denis Sassou Nguesso at their meeting

terms.explain: A rebel group fighting the government in eastern DR Congo.
Official relations between countries, like having ambassadors in each other's capitals.
A neutral person who helps two sides reach a deal.

stories.headline: UK PM Andy Burnham: rejoining the EU without a new referendum is "unthinkable"
stories.dek: Burnham plans to lay out options for closer ties with Europe next month, but says big steps would come only after the next election.
stories.caveman: In 2016, the UK voted in a referendum to leave the European Union, a move known as Brexit. Prime Minister Andy Burnham wants a much closer relationship with the EU and says Britain got a "bad Brexit deal." In Parliament on Monday, he was asked to promise he would never take the UK back into the EU without asking the public first. He answered: "Yes, it would be unthinkable." It is his strongest promise yet. He plans to set out long-term options next month, with real steps only after the next general election. Insiders expect that if he decides rejoining is best, he would ask for a mandate in his party's next election platform and then hold a confirming vote. He dismissed advice from former Conservative prime ministers Rishi Sunak, David Cameron and Theresa May not to reopen the Brexit debate, saying they are "stuck in the past." He says closer EU ties could help growth and lower energy bills.
stories.why_it_matters: Brexit changed trade, travel and work for millions of people. Whether Britain moves back toward Europe will shape its economy for years.
stories.camps: Pro-Europe voters welcome the promise of a public vote and closer ties. Brexit supporters say reopening the issue is divisive and ignores the 2016 result. Some pro-EU campaigners worry that requiring another referendum makes rejoining slower and harder.
stories.image_credit: Photo: Jack Hill/Reuters via The Guardian

terms.explain: The UK's exit from the European Union after the 2016 vote.
A vote where all citizens decide one specific question.
A group of 27 European countries that share trade rules and many laws.
Permission from voters to carry out a plan.

stories.headline: HOT TOPIC: 100+ writers break from PEN America to start a new group, citing Gaza
stories.dek: Ta-Nehisi Coates, M Gessen and Jacqueline Woodson are among the founders of "PEN Writes US."
stories.caveman: PEN America is a famous US group that defends writers and free speech. On Monday, more than 100 well-known writers and book people, including Ta-Nehisi Coates, M Gessen and Jacqueline Woodson, said they are forming a new group called PEN Writes US. It hopes to become an official PEN chapter with support from PEN International, joining more than 140 PEN centers around the world. The split comes after years of anger at PEN America's response to Israel's war in Gaza. Critics say it was slow to criticize Israel or defend Palestinian writers. Former PEN America president Francine Prose, now with the new group, said many felt the response had been "inadequate." The war already forced PEN America to cancel its awards and World Voices festival in 2024. Novelist Maaza Mengiste said the new group is not trying to be a rival, but wants "equal advocacy for all writers" over "institutional caution."
stories.why_it_matters: This is the biggest shake-up in the US literary world this year. It shows how the Gaza war is still dividing artists and institutions.
stories.camps: The new group's founders say PEN America failed to defend Palestinian writers equally. PEN America says it stays focused on defending free expression "regardless of viewpoint," and in June it published a report on harassment faced by Israeli and Jewish writers, which led its then-president to resign. Some writers worry a split weakens the fight against book bans and censorship.
stories.image_alt: The PEN America logo displayed at the PEN America literary awards in New York in 2023
stories.image_credit: Photo: Evan Agostini/Invision/AP via The Guardian

terms.explain: A US nonprofit that defends writers and free expression; part of the worldwide PEN network.
A smaller group that breaks away from a bigger one.
The right to speak, write and publish ideas without government punishment.

stories.headline: HOT: Pulitzer winner Richard Russo writes openly about his first panic attack
stories.dek: In a Lit Hub essay, the author of Empire Falls says OCD runs in his family and asks what else he has been ignoring.
stories.caveman: Richard Russo is one of America's most loved novelists; he won the Pulitzer Prize for Empire Falls and recently published a new novel, Under the Falls. In a new personal essay on Literary Hub, he describes waking up in the middle of the night this summer on Martha's Vineyard, shaking and in "a blind panic," afraid that if he took a ferry trip the next day he might never see his wife again. It was his first panic attack. He writes that he had felt anxious for a while about the world: a president he calls a "malignant narcissist," war in Iran, climate change, a possible pandemic, AI. But he also admits a deeper truth: obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) runs through his family. His grandmother had disabling panic attacks. He had assumed men in the family were spared. He writes about the stigma of saying "I'm mentally ill" and wonders what else he has missed or turned a blind eye to.
stories.why_it_matters: When a famous older man talks honestly about mental illness, it helps others feel less alone and less ashamed to seek help.
stories.camps: Many readers praise the essay's honesty. Some may find his political lines distracting from the personal story, while others say the outside world's chaos is exactly what triggers anxiety for many people, so it belongs in the piece.

terms.explain: A sudden wave of intense fear with physical symptoms like shaking, racing heart and trouble breathing.
Obsessive-compulsive disorder: unwanted repeated thoughts and urges that cause anxiety.
Shame or negative judgment attached to something, like mental illness.
A top US award for books, journalism and music.

stories.headline: NOT SO HOT: The Sun Also Rises turns 100, but students "don't like Hemingway"
stories.dek: A University of Iowa professor says Hemingway has fallen from academic grace, yet his novel about Americans abroad still has surprises.
stories.caveman: Ernest Hemingway's first big novel, The Sun Also Rises, came out in 1926, so it turns 100 this year. It follows a group of American and British expatriates (people living outside their home country) drinking and drifting through Paris and Spain, including the bullfights in Pamplona. In a Lit Hub essay, Harry Stecopoulos, who teaches literature at the University of Iowa, admits: "My students don't like Hemingway." They dislike his sexism, the "bulls, blood, and booze," and his macho "Papa" image. Over the past 40 years, he writes, Hemingway has fallen out of favor with scholars, and few people care about the anniversary. But he argues the book is stranger than its reputation: the narrator, Jake Barnes, has a war wound that left him impotent, and the novel is full of worry about masculinity and about what living abroad does to Americans, even hints of queerness.
stories.why_it_matters: Classics are always being re-read. How we judge old books, and whether we still teach them, says a lot about what each generation values.
stories.camps: Fans say Hemingway's simple, powerful style changed American writing forever and is still worth studying. Critics say his attitudes toward women and his macho myth have aged badly. This essay takes a middle path: read him critically, and you may find a more complicated, vulnerable book.
stories.image_alt: Illustration of a bullfighter and a bull, from Lit Hub's essay on The Sun Also Rises

terms.explain: A person living outside their home country.
Name for the group of American writers who came of age during World War I and many of whom lived in Paris in the 1920s.
Ideas about how men are "supposed" to act.

stories.headline: RISING: New history of the first big study of women's sex lives, from the 1920s
stories.dek: Historian Anya Jabour's Matters of Sex tells how Katharine Bement Davis surveyed 2,200 American women.
stories.caveman: In 1921, 20,000 American women opened a surprising letter from the Bureau of Social Hygiene in New York asking them, politely, to answer private questions about their sex lives. At the time, sex was barely discussed, and sex studies usually focused only on sex workers or people seen as "abnormal." About 1 in 10 replied: 1,000 married and 1,200 unmarried women. Their answers became Factors in the Sex Life of Twenty-Two Hundred Women (1929), by Katharine Bement Davis, one of the first American women to earn a PhD from the University of Chicago. A new book by historian Anya Jabour, Matters of Sex: Katharine Bement Davis and America's First Sexual Revolution (NYU Press), tells this story, and Lit Hub published an excerpt. Jabour says Davis's work was the first to put women's own experiences at the center and to treat female sexuality as normal, not shameful.
stories.why_it_matters: This is women's history that was almost forgotten. It shows how asking women directly, and believing them, can change science and society.
stories.camps: Many historians see Davis as a pioneer for women's health and honesty about sex. Others point out her study mostly reached well-off white women and came from a reform movement that also held some harsh views on morality. Both sides help explain both its importance and its limits.

terms.explain: A list of questions sent to many people to collect information.
A period when attitudes toward sex became more open.
A short section taken from a longer book.

stories.headline: Oxfam: Israel's war has turned Gaza into a "toxic wasteland" for decades
stories.dek: A new report finds poisoned water, contaminated soil and toxic air across the strip, from heavy metals, explosives, asbestos and sewage.
stories.caveman: A report by the charity Oxfam and the Conflict and Environment Observatory says Israel's military assault has contaminated the whole of Gaza. Using satellite images, remote sensing and scientific analysis, it found heavy metals, explosive residue, asbestos from destroyed buildings, and sewage polluting the air, soil and water. These toxins can reach people through what they breathe, eat and drink, and by touching rubble. The report says the danger could last for generations unless there is a major clean-up. The war has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians and wounded at least 175,000, with thousands still missing under rubble. Oxfam's director Amitabh Behar called the damage "environmental war crimes." A UN commission of inquiry has found Israel committed genocide in Gaza; Israel strongly rejects that finding.
stories.why_it_matters: Even after bombs stop, polluted water and soil keep making people sick, especially children. Rebuilding Gaza will mean cleaning the land itself, not just putting up buildings.
stories.camps: Aid groups and many governments say Israel must allow large-scale clean-up and reconstruction and be held accountable. Israel says its operations target Hamas, which it blames for using civilian areas, and rejects genocide accusations. Some critics of Oxfam say it takes sides; Oxfam says its findings are based on evidence.

terms.explain: When harmful substances get into air, water, soil or food.
A building material whose dust can cause deadly lung diseases.
Acts meant to destroy, in whole or in part, a national, ethnic, racial or religious group.
A large international charity that fights poverty and helps in disasters.

stories.headline: Iran whips a singer and her band 74 times each for performing without a hijab
stories.dek: Parastoo Ahmadi and four team members were also banned from music and travel for two years over an online concert video.
stories.caveman: In Iran, women must wear a hijab (head covering) in public by law. In December 2024, singer Parastoo Ahmadi posted a YouTube concert video in which she sang without a hijab, alongside male musicians, in the city of Qom. Iranian authorities charged her and four members of her production team with "offending public decency" by publishing "obscene and immoral content online." According to an Iranian news site quoting their lawyer, each of the five has now received 74 lashes, and all got two-year bans on artistic work and on travel. Western governments and human rights groups call flogging torture and a breach of international law. Iran rejects the criticism. The hijab rules became a flashpoint in 2022 after Mahsa Amini, a young Kurdish woman, died in police custody after being arrested over her dress. Since then, more women openly ignore the rules, and enforcement has become more selective.
stories.why_it_matters: This is about women's control over their own bodies and art. Punishing a singer for her hair sends a warning to every woman in Iran.
stories.camps: Human rights groups say the punishment is cruel and proves Iran is still cracking down on women. Iran's authorities say they are enforcing the country's laws and religious values, and accuse the West of hypocrisy about human rights. Inside Iran, many women keep pushing back by going uncovered.
stories.image_alt: Parastoo Ahmadi singing in her online concert video
stories.image_credit: Photo: Parastoo Ahmadi/YouTube via The Guardian

terms.explain: A head scarf worn by some Muslim women; required by law in public in Iran.
Hits with a whip as a legal punishment.
A 22-year-old woman whose 2022 death in Iranian police custody sparked nationwide protests.

stories.headline: Abusers are using smart car apps to track and control partners, researchers warn
stories.dek: Australian study finds risky remote features are common across major car brands; one man slowed his ex's car to 40 km/h.
stories.caveman: Many new cars can be controlled from a phone app: you can see where the car is, lock or unlock it, or limit how fast it goes. Researchers at the University of New South Wales in Australia found that these features are now common across major car brands and can be misused by domestic abusers. Their report lists real cases: a man in Australia was found guilty of using a car app to harass his ex-partner, including limiting her driving speed, sometimes to 40 km/h. In the US in 2022, a woman discovered her ex-husband was tracking her through her car's app, and the carmaker allegedly refused to cut off his access. The researchers say problems happen when the abuser owns the account, is added as a second user, or sets up an account pretending to be the victim. They urge carmakers to adopt "safety by design" so victims can easily remove someone's access.
stories.why_it_matters: Most domestic violence includes control, not just hitting. As homes and cars get "smarter," abusers get new tools to watch and trap people.
stories.camps: Researchers and victim support groups want carmakers to build in protections and respond fast when someone asks for help. Carmakers advertise these features as ways to protect the car or watch over family members. Privacy experts say the same feature can be safety or control, depending on who uses it.

terms.explain: Abuse by a partner or family member, including physical, emotional, financial and digital control.
Using phones, apps and devices to stalk, harass or control someone.
Building protections into a product from the start, not adding them after harm.

stories.headline: Nigeria boat carrying funeral mourners capsizes: at least 29 dead, 50 rescued
stories.dek: The overcrowded boat broke down; survivors say the operator refused to steer to land. Officials order stricter safety rules.
stories.caveman: In Nigeria, many people in villages near rivers travel by boat. On Friday, a boat carrying mourners to a funeral from the Ayama community had engine trouble. Police say passengers asked the operator to steer toward land, but he allegedly refused, and the boat capsized. So far, 29 bodies have been recovered and 50 people rescued, according to Nigeria's National Emergency Management Agency (Nema), and the search continues. Survivors described panic as people struggled to stay afloat. "Our things, our money, phones, everything lost, but me and my siblings are alive," one said. Nema said the boat was overcrowded but did not say how many were on board. Officials have raised worries about untrained boat operators and passengers without life jackets. The government has ordered stricter enforcement of safety rules on inland waterways.
stories.why_it_matters: Boat accidents kill many people in Nigeria every year, mostly poor rural families with few other ways to travel.
stories.camps: Officials blame overcrowding, bad maintenance and ignoring rules, and promise tougher enforcement. Local communities say they lack safe roads and affordable alternatives, and that enforcement alone will not help without investment in boats, training and life jackets.
stories.image_alt: Passengers crowded on a wooden boat on a river in Nigeria (file photo)

terms.explain: When a boat flips over in the water.
Rivers, lakes and canals used for travel inside a country.
Nigeria's National Emergency Management Agency, which handles disaster response.
